title: Acute Gastroenteritis in Children
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A common, usually viral, diarrhoeal illness in children that can lead to dehydration. Rapid assessment, rehydration and identification of bacterial or parasitic causes guide management, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Acute gastroenteritis (AGE) is diarrhoea lasting less than 14 days, often with vomiting, caused by viruses, bacteria or parasites. Diagnosis is clinical; stool culture is reserved for persistent or bloody diarrhoea.
The WHO dehydration scale guides treatment: no dehydration, some dehydration, severe dehydration. Clinical signs include dry mucous membranes, sunken fontanelle, lethargy, and capillary refill >2 s.
In East Africa the top causes are rotavirus, norovirus, bacterial pathogens (Shigella, Campylobacter, E. coli O157:H7) and parasites (Giardia, Entamoeba).
Children present with crampy abdominal pain, frequent loose stools, vomiting, fever (often <38.5°C), and signs of dehydration. Stool may be watery, mucoid or bloody.
Investigations are limited in low‑resource settings. Use them only when the diagnosis is unclear or complications are suspected.

t.b: Detects parasites and blood – a positive result suggests amoebiasis or dysentery
Confirms viral cause – useful if oral rehydration is sufficient
Assesses anemia and leukocytosis – leukocytosis may indicate bacterial infection
Identifies hyponatraemia or hyperkalaemia – guides fluid choice

sections.p: Urgent care is needed if the child is lethargic, has a fever >39°C, bloody stools, persistent vomiting, or signs of shock.

Treat the underlying cause if identified; otherwise provide supportive care. Oral rehydration solution (ORS) is first line. Zinc supplementation reduces duration. Antibiotics are reserved for bacterial causes.
b: ORS – 10–20 ml/kg over 1–2 h (severe) or 5–10 ml/kg every 15 min (moderate)
IV isotonic saline 20 ml/kg over 1 h (severe dehydration)

sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 24 h; ensure adequate fluid intake and nutrition. Preventive measures include hand hygiene, safe water, and rotavirus vaccination.
Severe malaria, typhoid fever, and acute appendicitis can mimic AGE but have distinct features such as fever spikes, rigors, or localized abdominal pain.
b: Appendicitis – right lower quadrant pain, rebound tenderness

sections.p: Stool microscopy may miss Giardia cysts; a negative test does not exclude bacterial infection. Serum electrolytes can be normal early in dehydration.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of shock (tachycardia, weak pulse, cold extremities)

faq.q: Why is zinc recommended for all children with AGE?
faq.a: Zinc shortens diarrhoea duration, reduces severity, and improves growth in children.

faq.q: When should IV fluids be started?
faq.a: In children with severe dehydration: sunken fontanelle, lethargy, delayed capillary refill >2 s.

faq.q: Can we give antibiotics for all cases of AGE?
faq.a: No; antibiotics are reserved for confirmed bacterial infections or severe cases with systemic signs.

exam: A 2‑year‑old presents with 3 days of watery diarrhoea and vomiting. He is lethargic and has a sunken fontanelle. What is the next step? — Assess dehydration severity, start IV isotonic saline, give ORS when stable.
A child with AGE has a fever of 39.5°C and bloody stools. Which pathogen is most likely? — Shigella; consider ciprofloxacin or azithromycin if confirmed.
Why is zinc not given to a child with severe dehydration? — Zinc is given orally; in severe dehydration the child needs IV fluids first.
A child with AGE has a normal stool microscopy but persistent diarrhoea >5 days. What is the next investigation? — Stool culture or PCR for bacterial pathogens.
Why is rotavirus vaccination important in East Africa? — It prevents the most common viral cause of AGE and reduces hospital admissions.
A child with AGE has hyponatraemia on serum electrolytes. What fluid should be used? — Isotonic saline; avoid hypotonic solutions to prevent cerebral oedema.
What is the WHO score for ‘some dehydration’ in a child? — 2–3 signs: sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, delayed capillary refill 2–3 s.
